newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Euro thoughts will dominate ISMA Singapore bash.
newsitem.headline: Euro thoughts will dominate ISMA Singapore bash.

text.p: Plane loads of bond traders have started to arrive in Singapore for their industry's annual bash, but during the odd moment between parties their thoughts will be back in Europe.

European economic and monetary union (EMU) is edging ever closer and bond traders are looking for answers as to what market conventions will be adopted to allow trade in the euro -- and they need these answers as soon as possible.
"Time is moving fast," John Langton, chief executive of the International Securities Market Association (ISMA), told Reuters before the start of its conference which runs from Wednesday until Friday.

"People need a minimum of 12 months notice (to make changes to their systems) for the euro, so we have to get recommendations out as soon as possible. Some will be released at the meeting on Thursday," he said.
The euro must be introduced no later than January 1, 1999 under European Union law. It is unclear which countries will take part and how strong the currency will be.
"EMU, the single currency and recommendations how we move to the new market in the smoothest possible manner need to be addressed," Langton said.

There are a myriad of concerns, with the question over successor price sources only one example. If a bond's return is based on a mark-based interest rate, what should its return be linked to once the mark no longer exists?
"If FIBOR (Frankfurt interbank offered rate) disappears, what do you do with a mark FRN?" asks Cliff Dammers, chairman of International Primary Market Association (IPMA).
"The market still has a lot of questions, and the focus (in Singapore) will be on EMU, EMU and EMU."
Representatives from both IPMA and ISMA have previously said the euro was likely to rival the dollar as the major international bond issuance currency.
As the practicalities of having to absorb a new currency sink in, bankers said EMU had taken some heat off ISMA's board.
Delegates said there was less time to fret about the internal workings of the ISMA, the international bond market's main self-regulatory body.

At the 1996 annual general meeting in Cannes, ISMA's board revealed the conclusions of a survey of its members, but the study was slated as unrepresentative and ISMA was criticised for not releasing the full results.

Among the issues raised was the possibility of changing the format of the AGM, considered by some as unnecessarily expensive and with too much focus on socialising and drinking, and demands were made for more accountability.
This year, ISMA did another study, which by all accounts will be better received by delegates.
"The follow-up to this year's questionnaire was very positive, with a fantastically high response rate," the head of one regional committee said.
"However, already since last year's survey, ISMA is using regional committees more. Perhaps the new survey will shift even more focus to them away from the central secretariat in Zurich," he said.
The results of ISMA's 1997 questionnaire will be presented on Thursday by Jose-Manuel Beneyto, the chairman of ISMA's regional representatives.

"Beneyto will give a half-hour presentation with the survey results," Langton said. "The survey is a follow-up to last year's. We had a very high response rate, and will publicly disclose and release all of the information. It will be very democratic."
Despite that, a senior banker in Luxembourg said: "There are still concerns about how ISMA makes decisions and whether the annual party is worth it."
"But concerns at banks are now more focused on the single currency. A lot of technical questions regarding EMU still need an answer, and the sooner they are resolved the better," he added.
The AGM will be followed by a conference on Friday, at which delegates will hear talks from Singapore's finance minister Richard Hu and former Australian prime minister Paul Keating.

Despite the need for a longer flight to reach this year's jamboree, many European delegates, who form by far the majority of participants, preferred the location to last year's bash on the French Riviera.

"Asian markets will grow in importance, and it will be useful to make contacts there," a bond trader at a European bank said. "A lot of people are combining the ISMA conference with business trips to Tokyo and Hong Kong."
"It makes more sense to organise it in Singapore, than somewhere like Cannes where there is no financial market at all."
-- Singapore newsroom (65) 870-3080
